posts.title: My Year On A Factory Floor Assembly Line

passages.text: When I was 19, I spent a year assembling electrical relays on a factory floor for $10/hr.
claims: At age 19, the author spent a year assembling electrical relays on a factory floor for $10 per hour.

passages.text: I was pretty excited to get the job.
claims: The author was excited to get the factory job.

passages.text: I’d been applying to much worse - I remember looking at at a craigslist ad for a sewage worker, which included a warning that it might be pretty gross. I applied for that too.
claims: Before getting the factory job, the author applied for a sewage-worker job after seeing a Craigslist ad that warned the work might be unpleasant.

passages.text: Knowingless is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
I really needed money.
claims: The author urgently needed money at the time.

passages.text: I was so poor I going hungry, would scrape change off the street for meals.
claims: The author was so poor that they went hungry and collected coins from the street to buy meals.

passages.text: I remember when touring a cheap room in northern Idaho to rent in a house full of strangers, they showed me the fridge, and I asked if people ever ate each other’s leftovers. They reassured me no, of course nobody would touch your food, and I was disappointed. That’s not what I had been trying to ask.
claims: While looking at an inexpensive room for rent in a shared house in northern Idaho, the author asked whether tenants ate one another’s leftovers, and felt disappointed when they were told that nobody would take their food; the author had meant to ask whether they could eat other tenants’ leftovers.

passages.text: I’d grown up in a very isolated, borderline-cult type of world where my parents had made it clear that they’d give me no financial assistance once I left home.
claims: The author grew up in an isolated environment they regarded as borderline cult-like, and their parents said they would provide no financial support after the author left home.

passages.text: Once you’re 18, you’re on your own, get a job, support yourself.
claims: The author's parents taught that a person should become independent, get a job, and support themselves at age 18.

passages.text: It didn’t even occur to me to let them know I was going hungry; I just figured that’s what happened to people when you were an adult.
claims: The author did not tell their parents they were going hungry because they assumed that going hungry was a normal part of adulthood.

passages.text: College wasn’t viable to me; I’d enrolled briefly but got kicked out after a few months once the finances didn’t work out.
claims: The author briefly enrolled in college but was removed after a few months when they could not make the finances work.

passages.text: A combination of my being homeschooled my entire life (weird transcripts), my parents making just too much money for me to qualify for financial aid while simultaneously refusing to cosign any loans at all, meant my path forward was not going to be one of education.
claims: The author says that being homeschooled, not qualifying for financial aid because of their parents’ income, and their parents’ refusal to cosign loans made continuing their education financially infeasible.

passages.text: So when Schweitzer Engineering Labs called to tell me I got the assembly line job at their Pullman manufacturing location, I was thrilled.
claims: The author was thrilled when Schweitzer Engineering Labs offered them an assembly-line job at its Pullman manufacturing location.

passages.text: It paid a full ten dollars an hour (in 2011).
claims: The assembly-line job paid the author $10 per hour in 2011.

passages.text: My last job, shelving books at the Nampa public library, had been $7.25 an hour.
claims: Before the factory job, the author shelved books at the Nampa public library for $7.25 per hour.

passages.text: And the assembly line job was indoors and I didn’t have to handle any poop! Amazing.
claims: The assembly-line job was indoors and did not require the author to handle feces.

passages.text: They said to show up at ~7am for training.
claims: The employer told the author to arrive at approximately 7 a.m. for training.

passages.text: I’d thought jobs usually started at 8am, and was disappointed that it was so early.
claims: The author expected jobs to start around 8 a.m. and was disappointed that this job started earlier.

passages.text: But I was grateful to have a job at all, and I was an adult now and I knew being an adult was supposed to be very difficult, so I said ‘okay’ and showed up at 7.
claims: The author was grateful to have a job, believed adulthood was supposed to be difficult, agreed to the early start, and arrived at 7 a.m.

passages.text: They put me and other new hires in a little room and we learned about the history of the company and how electrical relays worked and how the manufacturing floor functioned and then they showed us what all the tools were, how to screw and unscrew things, how to solder, etc.
claims: The author and other new hires received training on company history, electrical relays, factory operations, tools, fastening and unfastening components, and soldering.

passages.text: I liked learning things and I had a great time. I was determined to do awesome and I paid attention and tried super hard.
claims: The author enjoyed the training, paid close attention, and tried hard to perform well.

passages.text: After a few days training was over, I passed their mini tests with flying colors, and they said great - show up tomorrow at 6:30am.
claims: After a few days of training, the author passed the tests and was told to arrive at 6:30 a.m. the next day.

passages.text: I was oh wow. That’s kinda early.
claims: The author thought that a 6:30 a.m. start was early.

passages.text: They were like oh yeah right my bad, actually you’re on mandatory overtime, work starts at 5:30am.
claims: The employer told the author that they were on mandatory overtime and needed to start work at 5:30 a.m.

passages.text: I shortly find out that it’s only sometimes 5:30; much of my time working there required us clocking in before 5am.
claims: The author says that although the shift sometimes began at 5:30 a.m., much of their time at the job required clocking in before 5 a.m.

passages.text: Oh, and you have to work Saturdays. Sometimes if we’re really strapped, you need to come in on Sunday too.
claims: The author says the job required Saturday work and sometimes Sunday work when the factory was short-staffed.

passages.text: I lived 22 minutes away, so I spent my 19th year on this planet waking up at ~4:15am, getting home at 3:30pm, and going to sleep at 8pm, 6-7 days a week.
claims: During their 19th year, the author says they lived 22 minutes from work, woke at approximately 4:15 a.m., got home at 3:30 p.m., and went to bed at 8 p.m. six or seven days a week.

passages.text: I got assigned to a section near the end, where we put the relays into the metal boxes and wired then up.
claims: The author was assigned near the end of the production line, where workers put relays into metal boxes and wired them.

passages.text: Everything was on the same huge floor, the units just slowly flowed down the line and got shipped out the butt end of the building.
claims: The factory’s production work took place on one large floor, where units moved down the line and were shipped out from the far end of the building.

passages.text: There were no windows visible to us.
claims: The author and their coworkers could not see any windows from where they worked.

passages.text: When you arrive you get lockers where you put your stuff, and you have a little blue antistatic jacket/overcoat thing, and you put on special gloves and goggles and have to de-electrify yourself by plugging a wire from your coat into the wall.
claims: Workers at the factory stored their belongings in lockers, wore a blue antistatic garment, gloves, and goggles, and connected a wire from the garment to a wall outlet to discharge static electricity.

passages.text: Everything smelled SO specific, it’s hard to describe - like rubber and metal and other stuff I don’t have a term for.
claims: The author recalls that the factory had a distinctive smell, including scents they associated with rubber and metal.

passages.text: I was determined to have a good time.
claims: The author was determined to enjoy the job.

passages.text: I believed happiness was a choice, and if I just worked hard enough and was good and tried that things would go okay.
claims: The author believed that choosing happiness and working hard and behaving well would make things turn out successfully.

passages.text: I wanted to make everyone’s lives better, so I was annoyingly cheerful. Just downright homeschool-levels of goofy.
claims: The author wanted to improve other people’s lives and recalls being conspicuously cheerful and goofy.

passages.text: The units got passed down the floor on trays and these rubber pads.
claims: Units moved along the factory floor on trays and rubber pads.

passages.text: When I had a little downtime (which was rare and inadvised, they told us strictly that you should be finding something to do nonstop. If you are waiting for another assembler to finish their unit to pass to you, you should start immediately cleaning), I would scratch little cartoons or messages or silly things into the rubber pads.
claims: The author says that downtime was rare and discouraged, and workers were told to find tasks such as cleaning while waiting; during occasional downtime, the author scratched cartoons, messages, or other designs into rubber pads.

passages.text: They were very superficial and hard to see, you had to just catch the light reflecting off of them at the right angle to notice, and if you rub it really hard it fades away.
claims: The marks the author made on rubber pads were faint, visible only at certain angles of light, and faded when rubbed hard.

passages.text: I did this for weeks.
claims: The author made marks on the rubber pads for weeks.

passages.text: One day I came in and my team was in a special meeting, a rare huddle.
claims: The author recalls arriving one day to find their team holding an unusual meeting.

passages.text: All the teams on the entire floor were in their own huddles.
claims: All the teams on the factory floor were holding separate huddles.

passages.text: They gravely told us that someone had been VANDALIZING the equipment, and that they needed to find out who it is and that terrible vandal will have to replace everything - many thousands of dollars.
claims: The author’s team was told that someone had vandalized equipment, that management wanted to identify the person responsible, and that the person might have to pay thousands of dollars to replace the equipment.

passages.text: I was horrified and filled with shame.
claims: The author felt horrified and ashamed after hearing the announcement about vandalism.

passages.text: The next day I went to a company computer and emailed someone as high up as I could find (I think possibly the CEO?) admitting it was me and I’m sorry and I don’t know how I’ll be able to pay for it but I can try somehow, maybe take it out of my wages.
claims: The day after the announcement, the author emailed a senior company employee, possibly the CEO, admitted to making the marks, apologized, and offered to try to pay for the damage, perhaps through wage deductions.

passages.text: I never heard back; probably it got caught in some filter meant to prevent the plebians from reaching the consuls.
claims: The author says they received no reply to the email and speculates that a company filter may have blocked it.

passages.text: I did this on a break.
claims: The author sent the email during a work break.

passages.text: We got two legally-mandated 15 minute breaks (in addition to lunch).
claims: The author says workers received two legally mandated 15-minute breaks in addition to lunch.

passages.text: It was a big floor, and took a few minutes to walk into the break room, so the actual breaks were closer to like 9 minutes.
claims: The author says that walking to the break room reduced the effective length of each 15-minute break to about nine minutes.

passages.text: The lunches were generous; we got a full 45 minutes or hour, I forget.
claims: The author recalls that lunch breaks lasted either 45 minutes or an hour.

passages.text: They gave us free lunches on Fridays, where the entire company piled into the big special lunch room and we got some kind of presentation.
claims: The company provided free Friday lunches, during which employees gathered in a large lunch room and received presentations.

passages.text: There I got to see the other people who worked at the factory - not the assemblers, but the engineers, and the managers, and marketers, and whoever else.
claims: At the Friday gatherings, the author saw factory employees including engineers, managers, and marketers, rather than only assembly workers.

passages.text: I’d watch them longingly.
claims: The author watched the non-assembly employees with longing.

passages.text: I really wanted to be one of those.
claims: The author wanted to become a non-assembly employee such as an engineer, manager, or marketer.

passages.text: I had this idea that if I just worked really hard and really well on the factory floor, that eventually I could become one of them.
claims: The author believed that excellent work on the factory floor might eventually lead to a job like those held by engineers, managers, or marketers.

passages.text: I had some vague belief that I had a lot of potential.
claims: The author had a vague belief that they had considerable potential.

passages.text: I was vibrating with vision and an overactive mind.
claims: The author recalls having many ideas and an overactive mind.

passages.text: I thought I can do what they do but I have no idea how to get there.
claims: The author believed they could perform the work of the non-assembly employees but did not know how to reach those jobs.

passages.text: Eventually I figured out this wasn’t how it worked.
claims: The author eventually concluded that working hard on the factory floor would not automatically lead to the kind of job they wanted.

passages.text: The company advertised some educational program for assemblers to turn into brain people, but I couldn’t afford it.
claims: The company advertised an educational program intended to help assemblers move into professional roles, but the author could not afford it.

passages.text: I kept meeting coworkers who’d been on the assembly line floor for decades.
claims: The author met coworkers who had worked on the assembly line for decades.

passages.text: After many months I finally get pulled into a manager’s office for a performance review and they give me a 25 cent raise.
claims: After many months at the job, the author received a performance review and a 25-cent raise.

passages.text: I slowly lost hope.
claims: The author gradually lost hope.

passages.text: I really tried to hold on, but exhaustion made my fingers start slipping.
claims: The author tried to keep going, but exhaustion began to affect their dexterity.

passages.text: I was tired all the time.
claims: The author felt tired all the time.

passages.text: I got a friend to buy me some alcohol (19 years old remember) and started drinking many nights, which led to me being hungover and nonfunctional during the work hours.
claims: At age 19, the author had a friend buy alcohol for them and began drinking on many nights, leaving them hungover and unable to function well at work.

passages.text: I hateed the work.
claims: The author hated the factory work.

passages.text: It was a horrible no-good kind of work.
claims: The author regarded the work as extremely unpleasant.

passages.text: You couldn’t zone out and just do autopilot, because you had to follow a set of instructions with slight variations, that change a little each time.
claims: The assembly work required workers to follow instructions that varied slightly from unit to unit, making it difficult to work on autopilot.

passages.text: You had to pay attention.
claims: The assembly work required attention.

passages.text: But the attention you paid was not interesting; it was ongoing, it was relentless, it was stupid.
claims: The author found the attention required by the work uninteresting and relentless.

passages.text: My mind wasn’t mine, it was just barely pulled over some threshhold into a mind-killing, mundane amount of repetition.
claims: The author felt that the repetitive work deprived them of control over their own attention and thinking.

passages.text: I was bad at it.
claims: The author considered themselves poor at the assembly work.

passages.text: Before this I’d tended to be naturally good at almost everything I tried.
claims: Before the factory job, the author felt they had generally been good at most things they tried.

passages.text: I learned very fast.
claims: The author says they learned quickly.

passages.text: But here I made more mistakes than almost anyone else.
claims: The author says they made more mistakes on the factory job than nearly all their coworkers.

passages.text: They tracked mistakes; people spot-checked your work, and you got an anonymized code and you could go look at a leaderboard to see where your code ranked among others.
claims: The factory tracked workers’ mistakes through spot checks and used anonymous codes to display their relative rankings on a leaderboard.

passages.text: This depressed me more; how would I climb through the ranks and become an engineer if I accidentally screwed the blue wire onto the wrong node once every 200 times?
claims: The author felt more depressed about their prospects of becoming an engineer because they sometimes connected a blue wire to the wrong node, approximately once in every 200 instances.

passages.text: They didn’t want us to sit, and I think I started working there at the end of some kind of sitting war, because there were a few scattered chairs and angry muttering longtimers.
claims: The author recalls that management discouraged sitting and that, when they started, a few chairs remained and long-time workers muttered angrily, apparently after a dispute about sitting.

passages.text: Management thought sitting was bad and would destroy productivity, but some of the assemblers had fought back with cries of back pain, so they’d grudgingly allowed us a small number of chairs.
claims: The author says management believed sitting would reduce productivity, while some assemblers objected on the grounds of back pain, after which management allowed a small number of chairs.

passages.text: I was young, so did not get first access to a chair, but I loved it when I did.
claims: The author says they did not get priority access to chairs because they were young, but enjoyed sitting when they could.

passages.text: It made my day so so much better.
claims: Being able to sit substantially improved the author's day.

passages.text: Standing hurt, and made me worse at everything, and made me tired and sad.
claims: The author says standing caused pain, worsened their performance, and made them tired and sad.

passages.text: After a few months I got moved up the line, to the section where they installed the boards into the units.
claims: After a few months, the author was moved to a section of the production line where workers installed boards into units.

passages.text: This was less physically intensive, but more mentally draining.
claims: The author found the board-installation work less physically demanding but more mentally draining than their previous assignment.

passages.text: We assembled lots of different types of units, and the units went through different corresponding flow lines that had the required amount of tools.
claims: The factory assembled different types of units on corresponding production lines equipped with the tools needed for each line.

passages.text: But they wouldn’t let you sit and learn a single line, which might have one day allowed you to get used to it enough to zone out and have thoughts that were your own.
claims: The author says workers were not allowed to stay on one production line long enough to become familiar with it.

passages.text: No - you had to rotate spots regularly, so that you were always just slightly unfamiliar with your current task.
claims: Workers had to rotate positions regularly, which meant they were often somewhat unfamiliar with their current task.

passages.text: They did this so if people were out sick or something they could flexibly fill the gap, but it resulted in everyone being slightly worse at everything.
claims: The author says the company rotated workers so they could cover for absent colleagues, but believes the rotation made workers less proficient at each task.

passages.text: There was no groove to fall into.
claims: The author says the changing assignments prevented workers from settling into a familiar routine.

passages.text: It was an infinite series of tiny tasks that changed a little bit all the time, and a lot sometimes, and if you fail someone might DIE.
claims: The author describes the work as a succession of small tasks that varied, and says that an assembly error could potentially cause someone's death.

passages.text: And then randomly you’d get thrown into the picker role, which meant you spent the day working in the warehouse.
claims: Workers could be assigned unpredictably to the picker role, which involved spending the day in the warehouse.

passages.text: You’d have to haul in a big stacked tray on wheels and go down a list of paper and then run around the shelves pulling boxes off and scanning them and hauling the tray back.
claims: The picker role involved moving a loaded wheeled tray through the warehouse, selecting and scanning boxes according to a paper list, and returning the tray.

passages.text: This was awesome cause it meant at least you weren’t standing still, but it was physically exhausting and happened rarely enough you never got used to it.
claims: The author enjoyed that picker work involved moving around rather than standing still, but found it physically exhausting and says it occurred too rarely for workers to get used to it.

passages.text: Throughout it all, I was still grateful.
claims: The author remained grateful while working at the factory.

passages.text: I saved most of my money, and felt like a king sitting on a savings account of a few thousand dollars.
claims: The author saved most of their earnings and accumulated savings of a few thousand dollars.

passages.text: I was happy I was not working in poop.
claims: The author was glad their job did not involve handling feces.

passages.text: I was happy to not be hungry.
claims: The author was glad they were no longer hungry.

passages.text: But even so, the depression slowly crept around me and I had this sense that I did not want to spend the rest of my life like this.
claims: The author says they gradually became depressed and did not want to spend the rest of their life doing the factory work.

passages.text: I was so confused by the coworkers that had been there for a decade+ and seemed content with their lives.
claims: The author was puzzled by coworkers who had worked at the factory for more than a decade and seemed content.

passages.text: I thought we were all on a ship that had rescued us from the void and we were so thankful and just waiting for the ship to deliver us to better lands, and so why were you still on the boat?
claims: The author imagined the workers as people rescued from hardship who were waiting for better opportunities, and wondered why long-term coworkers remained at the factory.

passages.text: Why had you not gotten off?
claims: The author wondered why coworkers who had worked at the factory for a long time had not left.

passages.text: They were all poor.
claims: The author regarded their coworkers as poor.

passages.text: I had a few coworkers my age; one had come from a farm, the other wanted to do college but hadn’t managed to make it for some reason.
claims: The author had a few coworkers of similar age; one came from a farm, and another wanted to attend college but had not managed to do so.

passages.text: Some were divorced moms, others jolly church guys.
claims: The author says some coworkers were divorced mothers and others were cheerful men associated with a church.

passages.text: We all shopped at wal-mart and used coupons for groceries.
claims: The author says they and their coworkers shopped at Walmart and used grocery coupons.

passages.text: I wondered about their lives outside of this, but there probably wasn’t actually that much life outside of this.
claims: The author wondered about coworkers’ lives outside work and suspected they had little time or activity beyond the factory.

passages.text: We were with each other for the majority of our waking hours.
claims: The author and coworkers spent most of their waking hours together.

passages.text: The factory walled us in both in space and time.
claims: The author felt that the factory constrained workers’ lives both spatially and temporally.

passages.text: I started calling in sick more often.
claims: The author began calling in sick more frequently.

passages.text: Sometimes I’d wake up and stare at the ceiling and just completely lack the will to make myself get up and go to work.
claims: The author sometimes woke up unable to summon the motivation to get out of bed and go to work.

passages.text: I started bumping up against management who frowned at me for taking so many days off.
claims: The author began having difficulties with management, who disapproved of the number of days off the author took.

passages.text: My compulsive please-authority streak was not strong enough to force me out of bed, often hungover, into yet another 9-10.5 hours under flourescent lights on a Saturday.
claims: The author says their tendency to obey authority did not make them go to work on some Saturdays, when they were often hungover and faced another 9 to 10.5-hour shift under fluorescent lights.

passages.text: I got out because I got another job.
claims: The narrator left the factory job because they got another job.

passages.text: I’d been watching other job ads on craigslist and saw one opening for a boudoir photographer.
claims: The narrator had been looking at job advertisements on Craigslist and saw an opening for a boudoir photographer.

passages.text: I liked taking photos of my pretty friends on weekends, and  so I applied, and showed them all the pretty photos I’d taken, and one day after work when I was in a hardware store they called me to tell me I was hired.
claims: The narrator applied for a boudoir photographer job, showed the employers photos they had taken of friends, and was told they were hired while at a hardware store after work.

passages.text: I almost died of joy.
I told everyone at the assembly line I was getting out, and they were so happy for me.
claims: The narrator told their assembly-line coworkers they were leaving, and the coworkers were happy for the narrator.

passages.text: I remember my last day clearing out my locker and walking out for the very last time and they were congratulating me and wishing me luck and then I was gone.
claims: On the narrator’s last day at the factory, they cleared out their locker and left while coworkers congratulated them and wished them luck.

passages.text: I went to the clothing store and asked the lady working there to suggest office clothes for me, because I was going to be a professional now.
claims: The narrator went to a clothing store, asked an employee to suggest office clothes, and intended to start working in a professional role.

passages.text: She handed me a set of clothes and I bought them all.
claims: A clothing-store employee gave the narrator a set of clothes to consider, and the narrator bought all of them.

passages.text: No more blue antistatic factory coat!
claims: The narrator no longer had to wear a blue antistatic coat for factory work.

passages.text: The photography job lasted two weeks.
claims: The narrator’s photography job lasted two weeks.

passages.text: I’d just turned 20 and I’d been homeschooled my whole life and I had no idea how to interact with people where I was in a role of authority.
claims: When the narrator began the photography job, they had recently turned 20, had been homeschooled throughout their life, and did not know how to interact with people while in a position of authority.

passages.text: I’d had all fire quite literally beaten out of me and was compulsively submissive, quiet, nervous.
claims: The narrator says they had been physically beaten and had become compulsively submissive, quiet, and nervous.

passages.text: I was not good at making strangers feel sexy and like I had everything under control in photoshoots.
claims: The narrator says they were not good at making strangers feel sexy or making it seem that they had everything under control during photoshoots.

passages.text: The boss called me into his office and said sorry, we need to let you go.
claims: The narrator’s boss called them into his office and told them they were being let go.

passages.text: I said okay.
claims: The narrator replied, “okay,” when their boss told them they were being let go.

passages.text: I understand.
claims: The narrator told their boss they understood that they were being let go.

passages.text: I walked out, wearing my ill-fitting ‘office’ clothes I’d bought for this job, climbed into my beat-up little car, and wailed like death the entire drive home.
claims: After being let go, the narrator left wearing the office clothes they had bought for the job, got into their car, and cried loudly throughout the drive home.

passages.text: This was my one shot out into a better life and I’d blown it.
claims: The narrator believed that the photography job had been their only chance to improve their life and that they had ruined that chance.

passages.text: I had no idea what I was going to do, but I knew no matter what happened, I would not return to the ship that had rescued me from the void.
claims: After losing the photography job, the narrator did not know what to do next but was determined not to return to the ship they described as having rescued them from the void.

passages.text: I would do anything but that.
claims: The narrator was determined to do anything rather than return to the ship they had left.

passages.text: I had a little bit of savings to sustain me for some months, and so I began trying and failing, trying and failing, over and over again, until one day I met a man off okcupid who asked if I’d ever heard of this thing called webcamming.
claims: The narrator had enough savings to support them for several months, repeatedly tried and failed at unspecified pursuits, and eventually met a man on OkCupid who asked whether they had heard of webcamming.

passages.text: Most of the nightmares I ever have are about the factory floor.
claims: The narrator says that most of their nightmares are about the factory floor.

passages.text: I dream I have to go back for some reason, I’ve lost my job, I have to go recover something and they need my help and I get sucked in.
claims: The narrator often dreams that they have to return to the factory after losing their job, recover something, and help the people there, and that they become trapped there again.

passages.text: It’s strange for that place to be such a nightmare for me - so many other people are working there, right now as you read this, and presumably they do not feel like they’re in a nightmare.
claims: Many people work at the factory, and the narrator supposes that they do not experience working there as a nightmare.

passages.text: Maybe they’re good at their jobs.
claims: The narrator speculates that the factory workers may be good at their jobs.

passages.text: They get decent health insurance and plenty of money for groceries and a free lunch every Friday.
claims: The factory workers receive health insurance the narrator considers decent, enough money for groceries, and a free lunch every Friday.

passages.text: Am I weak, for failing to endure what others can thrive on?
Is something in me so brittle I had to drink to coat my exposed nerves?
I don’t know.
But I think about them a lot, and I hope one day we can get a nicer, bigger boat to rescue them again.
